As the RRF enters its crucial final phase, we take stock of the situation with Pierre Moscovici, the French member of the European Court of Auditors (ECA).

Geopolitics.summary: On January 30, 2026, the US Justice Department released 3 million documents. Photos, videos, emails, text messages, court records... All connected to one man: Jeffrey Epstein. Since then, media outlets around the world have brought to light the vast amount of people that appear in the Epstein files. Eight months on, what what do these revelations tell us about Jeffrey Epstein’s network? How did it operate? FRANCE 24 journalist Ava Luquet spent months digging through the files. Geopolitics.title: Labour hails byelection win as return of leftwing voters after Starmer era
Geopolitics.summary: Party now polling 15 points above Greens, who had been ahead of Labour before Keir Starmer resigned as PM Labour is starting to win back voters on the left who became disillusioned under Keir Starmer’s leadership, the party’s deputy leader has claimed after it saw off Zack Polanski and the Greens to win the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. Geopolitics.summary: State planning minister declares project ‘state significant’, wresting approval process away from local council Plans for a grand new public square in the centre of Sydney are in doubt after the New South Wales planning minister declared the project “state significant”, wresting the approval process away from the City of Sydney. Geopolitics.title: Lawsuits blame Fox News for deaths of journalists in Ukraine
Geopolitics.summary: This week, FRANCE 24's media show Scoop revisits a fatal assignment for a Fox News team in Ukraine. On March 14, 2022, a Russian strike hit the crew reporting near the capital Kyiv. Reporter Benjamin Hall was seriously injured and two other journalists were killed. The journalists' families are suing Fox, saying the network put the story ahead of its people. Our guest is NPR's David Folkenflik.

Geopolitics.title: 'Absolute torture': Female US inmate in critical condition after botched execution
Geopolitics.summary: A condemned female murderer who survived two lethal injections during a botched execution by the US state of Tennessee was in critical condition and receiving "life-saving care," according to her attorneys. In an extraordinary chain of events, Christa Pike, 50, was whisked from a prison execution chamber to a hospital, still alive despite two deadly doses of pentobarbital. What happened to Pike is "absolute torture," said Sandrine Ageorges-Skinner, Spokesperson for Together Against the Death Penalty (ECPM), speaking to FRANCE 24's Alison Sargent.

Geopolitics.title: New York City’s Marble Hill residents furious after ICE shooting: ‘Why do this?’
Geopolitics.summary: Locals also express fear after man shot in the neck while his child was in the back of his car Residents of Manhattan’s Marble Hill neighborhood were furious at federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Friday but also scared after an officer shot their neighbor who had his child in the back of his car. Geopolitics.summary: It has been dubbed "the PISA shock". Countries that had been used to their school pupils performing well in test scores are seeing a plunge in standards. The PISA test is an international assessment led by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which measures how well 15‑year‑olds in over 80 countries apply reading, mathematics and science skills to real‑world problems. In the latest rankings, France's results were the worst it has ever had, and Germany's school pupils got their worst PISA report card too.

Geopolitics.summary: The new leader of the Islamic Community in Bosnia and Herzegovina will be elected on October 10. The reis-ul-ulema's role is not only important for Muslims in the country itself, but could inspire Muslims across Europe.

Geopolitics.title: Italy's biggest-ever wine heist
Geopolitics.summary: A multi million euro wine heist in Italy. As thieves in Tuscany steal 30 thousand bottles of the one of the most iconic labels in the country from a warehouse of the the prized Marchesi Antinori winery as it prepared for a major export. The company said in the past few hours, they believe two vans and up to six thieves were involved. Gavin Lee speaks to France 24's correspondent in Rome, Seema Gupta.

Geopolitics.summary: An astronaut crew that carried out an eight-month mission aboard the International Space Station splashed down as planned Thursday off the coast of California. Geopolitics.title: Sierra Leone: From 'blood diamonds' to stones of hope?
Geopolitics.summary: "Blood diamonds" became infamous for funding the brutal civil war in Sierra Leone. Beginning 25 years ago, the Kimberley Process aimed to put an end to this illegal trade. Accused of complicity in the conflict, the diamond industry has since sought to clean up its image, emphasising an ethical shift. But a quarter of a century on, have the former "blood diamonds" truly become synonymous with development? FRANCE 24's Sarah Sakho and Simon Martin report.

Geopolitics.title: Callum Turner's new film sparkles at Dinard Film Festival
Geopolitics.summary: British and Irish cinema have been in the spotlight at the Breton resort of Dinard for more than three decades, with films like "The Full Monty" and "Billy Elliot" getting their starts at the town's annual film festival. FRANCE 24's Culture editor Eve Jackson brings us the latest from this year’s edition, from its line-up to the financial woes that could spell the end of the festival.

Geopolitics.summary: Species with leaves large enough to be seen from space is already critically endangered – and plans are afoot to protect it A chance social media encounter has led to the race-against-time discovery of a new species of giant waterlily that has until now been hidden in the depths of Colombia’s jungle. But the plant, which is so huge it is visible from space, is already considered critically endangered. Continue reading...

Geopolitics.title: Crazy Rich Asians to return as TV show with original film's stars
Geopolitics.summary: It will pick up after the hit 2018 film, starring Constance Wu, Henry Golding, Michelle Yeoh and Ronny Chieng.

Science.title: NASA astronauts splash down after 100 million miles in space
Science.summary: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 astronauts have returned to Earth after 237 days in space, traveling more than 100 million miles and completing over 3,792 orbits while conducting research to prepare for future missions to the Moon and Mars. The mission also made history with record-setting spacewalk achievements and experiments that could transform medicine both in space and on Earth.

Science.title: The oil market that sets today's gas prices was invented in western Pennsylvania
Science.summary: The fall of 2026 is a moment when energy takes center stage, as geopolitics unfolding far away shows up in Americans' everyday lives.

Science.title: Geologists uncover evidence of a missing Late Cretaceous magmatic arc in northwestern Iran
Science.summary: Mountains preserve evidence of ancient oceans, moving continents and tectonic processes that have shaped Earth over millions of years. Later deformation, erosion and burial, however, can obscure important parts of this geological record. An international research team led by Istanbul Technical University (ITU) has identified evidence of a previously unrecognized Late Cretaceous continental magmatic arc in northwestern Iran.

Science.title: Some climate tipping points are being studied far more than others
Science.summary: Parts of Earth's climate system can change abruptly once warming pushes them beyond critical thresholds. The Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, the Amazon rainforest, coral reefs and major ocean currents are all among the systems containing potential climate tipping points.

Science.title: A 9-billion-year-old signal could help explain dark energy
Science.summary: A Canadian radio telescope has detected the faint glow of hydrogen from billions of years ago using only its own observations, proving a long-awaited way to map the distant universe can actually work. CHIME can use this hydrogen signal to trace how matter is spread across space and measure how the universe has expanded over time, offering a powerful new way to investigate dark energy.

Science.title: Climate change drives new species combinations, prompting calls to rethink conservation goals
Science.summary: The fact that ecosystems change is nothing new. What is new, however, is the speed and scale at which new species communities are emerging as a result of climate change. Processes that once unfolded over centuries or even millennia are now being observed within just a few decades.

Science.title: Strong magnetic fields could allow white dwarfs to grow beyond the Chandrasekhar limit
Science.summary: When a dying star runs out of fuel and sheds its outer layers, its remaining core can become an approximately Earth-sized, extremely dense stellar remnant called a white dwarf. For a white dwarf that is not strongly rotating or magnetized, there is a well-known upper mass limit of about 1.4 times the mass of the sun, known as the Chandrasekhar limit.

Science.title: Aspens 'remember' past drought in their leaves, 3-year experiment finds
Science.summary: Drought is written into trees, appearing as narrow bands in their annual growth rings. But aspen may go farther, creating "functional memories" of previous dry years reflected in the chemistry of their leaves, according to new research by University of Utah biologists.

Science.title: Researchers call for national consortium to battle agriculture cyber threats
Science.summary: The threat of cyberattacks against American agriculture and food systems is growing, and Washington State University researchers are helping to lead a call for a national consortium of land-grant universities to study and combat the threat.

Science.title: African antelopes spreading in New Mexico: How far could they go under climate change?
Science.summary: Majestic African antelopes known as gemsbok have been roaming the U.S. Southwest since their introduction in the 1960s and 1970s. Brought to New Mexico as a game species for hunting, gemsbok quickly settled in, expanding more than 100 kilometers (62 miles) from their introduction point. University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign researchers say that's due to their exceptional adaptations to arid conditions, which they predict will dramatically expand under climate change.

Science.title: Polar oceans store carbon—but policy is not yet ready to count it
Science.summary: Polar oceans may play an important role in storing carbon and supporting biodiversity, but current science and policy frameworks are not yet ready to fully recognize their potential.

Science.title: AI reveals how coating thickness changes the link between surface roughness and pitting resistance
Science.summary: Localized pitting corrosion can cause sudden failure in aluminum components even when overall corrosion rates are low. Steam coating offers a water-vapor-based route to protective boehmite films, but processing simultaneously changes film thickness, surface morphology, crystallinity and substrate defects.

Science.title: Discovery marks the first detection of variable water clouds outside of the solar system
Science.summary: A Jupiter-sized world just 7.5 light-years away is cloudy, chemically complex and, it turns out, more like home than anyone expected. Using the James Webb Space Telescope, Brittany Miles, assistant astronomer at the University of Arizona's Steward Observatory, led a team that spent 11 hours staring at WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf, collecting a spectrum of its light every 15 minutes.

Science.title: Q&A: How does AI affect our engagement at work?
Science.summary: AI is being integrated into our work at a growing rate. Andreas Bergqvist, a Ph.D. student at the Department of Information Technology, has teamed up with colleagues to investigate how AI, automation and robotization affect work engagement.

Science.title: Plant-bacteria partnership reveals how roots access iron locked in soil
Science.summary: A new study led by Paul Schulze-Lefert from the Max Planck Institute for Plant Breeding Research in Cologne, in collaboration with Ricardo F.H. Giehl at the Leibniz Institute of Plant Genetics and Crop Plant Research in Gatersleben, revealed how Arabidopsis plants adapt their chemical communication with the bacterial root microbiota to maximize the acquisition of bio-unavailable iron from acidic or calcareous soils. The study is now published in Cell.

Science.title: Scientists discover 180,000 giant tortoises on one Seychelles island
Science.summary: Free-roaming Aldabra population far exceeds human population of Seychelles after decades-long recovery programme A survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has discovered that the once endangered species is thriving. A population of Aldabra giant tortoises lives on an island in Seychelles called Aldabra Atoll. Continue reading...

Science.title: 'Freakish' discovery of 9 million-year-old capybara tooth supports idea that Atacama wasn't always a desert
Science.summary: A 9 million-year-old capybara tooth was found in the Atacama Desert, a surprising find given that these rodents love water.

Science.title: Scientists find hidden materials that could improve batteries and solar fuels
Science.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden world of “in-between” materials that briefly form as chemical ingredients are heated, revealing structures that conventional methods can miss. Among the discoveries is a previously unknown form of bismuth vanadate, a material widely studied for using sunlight to help produce clean hydrogen. The new version has a different atomic structure and interacts with light in a strikingly different way, potentially opening new possibilities for solar fuels, catalysts, and electronics.

Science.title: New sensing method expands label-free particle detection beyond sensor surfaces
Science.summary: Finding a single cancer cell in a tube of blood is a bit like finding a needle in a haystack. As researchers seek to detect ever-smaller and rarer targets, from viruses to circulating tumor cells in blood, the demand for ultrasensitive, robust sensors that are practical for real-world samples continues to grow.

Science.title: Bacteria turn a virus’ own weapon against it
Science.summary: Researchers have uncovered a new way bacteria detect viral attacks: a virus-produced enzyme cuts a bacterial sensor protein, triggering a self-destructing immune response. The discovery could lead to more effective phage therapies against antibiotic-resistant bacteria and provide insight into ancient immune mechanisms shared with humans.

Science.title: Food testing reveals how diet can add to exposure to 'forever chemicals'
Science.summary: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)—a vast family of chemicals used largely for their nonstick, water-repellent and grease-resistant properties—are called "forever chemicals" because of their remarkable resistance to degradation. They are now ubiquitous in our environment.

Science.title: South Korean 'robot dog' became first to run a marathon on a single battery charge — now we know how
Science.summary: A quadruped robot scampered more than 26.2 miles of uneven, hilly terrain alongside human runners without needing to be recharged.

Science.title: Quantum chip holds multiple photons at once, opening path to scalable memory
Science.summary: For highly fragile quantum information systems, the ability to store quantum information is vital—but also challenging. Quantum information is transported in particles of light called photons, which often must be temporarily paused (or "stored") while other, slower quantum operations catch up. This storage must be performed on microchips as small as 1 centimeter (0.4 inches)—a distance covered by light in a few trillionths of a second. Storing photons for a microsecond would represent a massive leap forward for the capabilities of quantum chips.

Science.title: NASA advances LISA mission contributions with new test telescope
Science.summary: NASA has taken the next step in the process of developing a new all-glass telescope for the LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) mission, a space observatory designed to detect ripples in space-time called gravitational waves.

Science.title: Chimp and gorilla brains resist weight loss with age — unlike human brains
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 09 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03158-0 The relatively short lifespans of non-human great apes might explain why their brain mass is maintained in later life

Science.title: A quantum prediction from 1931 just came to life
Science.summary: Nearly a century after physicist Hans Bethe predicted them, scientists have created and directly observed unusual quantum states known as “Bethe strings” in an ultracold gas. By cooling cesium atoms to near absolute zero and trapping them in thousands of tiny one-dimensional tubes, researchers were able to make groups of atoms bind together without ordinary chemical bonds. These strange clusters could contain six or more particles and even collide with one another without falling apart.

Science.title: Genetic analysis reveals that some specialty coffee seeds do not match their commercial identity
Science.summary: Genetic analysis revealed that several seeds from a batch sold as Sidra were not, in fact, Sidra; their genetic profile was closer to that of Batian, a Kenyan variety.

Science.title: Nightjar wings reveal a trade-off between hunting slowly and traveling far
Science.summary: The European nightjar (Caprimulgus europaeus) is a nocturnal migratory bird that travels between Europe and southern Africa each year. However, its wings are not only used for long-distance journeys. When hunting insects, the nightjar must be able to slow down, turn sharply and fly at low speeds. Researchers at Lund University have now shown how this trade-off is reflected in the bird's flight mechanics. The study is published in the journal PLOS Biology.

Science.title: Fluorescent imaging tracks metabolism of cells in real time
Science.summary: Cornell researchers have designed a new, faster form of two-photon fluorescence imaging for observing cell metabolism in real time, a method that could enable quicker screening of new therapeutic treatments. The findings were published Sept. 4 in Science Advances. The co-lead authors are former postdoctoral researcher Lu Ling, Ph.D. '20, and doctoral student Jack Crowley, M.S. '22.

Science.title: Breaking down nerve-cell scaffold relieves chronic pain in mice
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 09 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03159-z Results could help researchers to develop painkillers that are safer and more effective than existing treatments.

Science.title: Cool chemistry trick allows new tattoos to 'turn on and off'
Science.summary: Researchers created multicolored tattoo inks that are activated by different wavelengths of light, allowing people to hide their tattoos in different scenarios.

Science.title: Watch this invisible tattoo appear under UV light
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 09 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03210-z The ink could be useful for medical tattooing, but more tests are needed before it is widely available.

Science.title: Adjustable nanosensors turn water pressure into fluorescent signals, with stiffness shaping sensitivity
Science.summary: A novel nanovesicle-based platform developed at Institute of Science Tokyo can measure hydrostatic pressure by converting pressure-induced molecular changes into fluorescence signals.

Science.title: October’s night sky is full of cosmic tricks and treats
Science.summary: October’s skies are packed with celestial surprises, from Jupiter disappearing behind the Moon to two meteor showers lighting up the darkness. NASA highlights four must-see events, including shooting stars from Halley’s Comet and a glowing Hunter’s Moon just before Halloween.

Science.title: Cyberbullying rarely occurs in isolation—it functions as an extension of school violence, say researchers
Science.summary: A new study of 4,200 adolescents revealed that cyberbullying rarely occurs in isolation; it almost always functions as an extension of physical and verbal aggression already present in the school environment. The study, conducted at the Federal University of São Paulo (Unifesp) in Brazil, mapped students' involvement in bullying and found that the lines between victims and perpetrators often blur in a cycle of violence spanning both the physical and digital worlds.

Science.title: What a swordfish washing up on British Columbia's coast says about our changing oceans
Science.summary: Filmmaker and outdoorsperson Quinn Barabash recently made headlines when he found a swordfish carcass nearly two meters (6.6 feet) long on the remote shores of Haida Gwaii in northern British Columbia.

Science.title: Webb telescope detects galaxy origin of the farthest fast radio burst we've seen to date
Science.summary: Astronomers used the Webb telescope to see where the farthest fast radio burst we've ever seen had come from.

Science.title: Scientists have identified a 'protein signature' in blood that could predict healthy aging
Science.summary: Having a certain ratio of proteins produced by immune cells in your blood is linked to a higher risk of age-related diseases, scientists report.

Science.title: Bronze ring with Lighthouse of Alexandria engraving discovered at palace on submerged island in Egypt
Science.summary: A bronze ring that depicts the Lighthouse of Alexandria has been discovered underwater in the remains of an ancient palace.

Science.title: The life of Darwin and the science of clouds: Books in brief
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 09 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03217-6 Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

Science.title: Five movements from the edge of the singularity
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 09 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03116-w Change is in the air.

Science.title: Kīlauea's swelling summit helps scientists forecast lava fountain eruptions
Science.summary: Episodic lava fountaining is a rare volcanic behavior in which repeated, hours-long bursts of molten lava and gas are spewed from volcanic vents, with quiet pauses lasting days to weeks between episodes. These lava fountains have been observed in active volcanoes in places like Hawaii, Iceland and Italy, but researchers still do not fully understand what starts, sustains or stops these individual fountain episodes.

Science.title: Two large asteroids found spinning as fast as a fairground ride
Science.summary: Rocks in the asteroid belt rotating at ultra-fast speeds suggest our understanding of asteroid structure might be wrong

Science.title: 'October is the ideal time to get vaccinated': Flu season is kicking off early, experts say
Science.summary: Flu tests are coming back positive at higher rates than is typical for early fall in several Western states, data suggests.

Science.title: 'Mix-and-match' material's properties can be tuned by changing its metallic 'recipe'
Science.summary: Scientists have created a new family of materials whose behavior can be tuned by changing their metallic "recipe"—opening new possibilities for uses including gas storage and sensing.

Science.title: Big dogs age faster at an epigenetic level, new study finds
Science.summary: A new study that tracked dogs' aging by reading tiny chemical tags on their DNA found that larger dogs aged more quickly.

Science.title: Three quantum-inspired cores leave opposite fingerprints on the ringing of black holes
Science.summary: Every black hole hides a question at its center. Einstein's theory predicts that whatever falls in is crushed into a singularity, a point of infinite density where the theory itself breaks down. Most physicists expect quantum gravity to replace that point with something finite. But the center lies hidden behind the horizon. How could we ever learn what is there?

Science.title: Confidence in a relationship's future is linked to feelings of romantic security
Science.summary: Feeling secure in a relationship is not only about how people connect with their partners today. It may also depend on how confident they are that the relationship will continue into the future. Feelings of closeness, trust and connection, together with a sense that the relationship is stable and has a future, can shape how people experience their romantic relationships.

Science.title: Data centers make heat all year long—here's how the ground can hold onto it until winter
Science.summary: You have probably noticed it on a hot summer day: A basement feels cool even when the air outside is baking. The ground does not heat up and cool down as fast as the air does. A few hundred feet down, it stays close to the local yearly average all year, which can be around 50 degrees Fahrenheit (10 degrees Celsius).
